title: AP English Language and Composition
summary: Build rhetorical analysis, synthesis and argument through nine applied reading and writing cycles.
frameworkNote: 2026–27 structure checked against College Board on 15 October 2026: 9 units. Original VertexED focused lessons and self-check questions sample each unit; they do not replace the full course framework, required materials or teacher review. College Board organises this course into nine numbered skill cycles without fixed topic titles. Module titles here are original teaching labels. All example sentences are original, not exam passages.

modules.title: Claims, reasons and audience
modules.focus: Identify what a writer wants readers to believe or do.
explanation: A claim is an arguable position, while a reason explains why it should be accepted. Evidence supports that reason through examples, observations or data. A summary restates a position; analysis explains how the parts work together.

Rhetorical situation includes speaker, audience, purpose and context. The same evidence can have different force for different readers. Avoid simply naming ethos, pathos or logos without explaining a particular choice and its likely effect.

workedExample.prompt: Original example: “Keep the library open later; evening workers cannot visit before closing.” Analyse the reasoning.
steps: The claim asks for longer opening hours.
The reason links current hours to unequal access, appealing to readers concerned with community provision.

misconception.claim: Every factual statement is an argument.
misconception.correction: An argument connects evidence and reasoning to a debatable claim.

questions.prompt: What evidence would strengthen the library claim?
questions.answer: Visitor surveys or work-schedule data showing unmet evening demand would support the stated reason.

questions.prompt: Why might a budget committee need more evidence than current library users?
questions.answer: The committee must weigh staffing costs and alternatives, so demand evidence should be paired with a feasible cost analysis.

questions.prompt: Original invented sentence: 'Publish the meal ingredients so pupils can choose safely.' Identify the claim, reason and audience.
questions.hint: Separate the requested action from its purpose.
hints: Separate the requested action from its purpose.
Identify who can publish the information.
questions.answer: The claim asks the catering team or school to publish ingredients; the reason is safer informed choices for pupils.
checkpoints: Identify safer choice as the reason.

questions.prompt: A student addresses the same ingredient proposal to a finance committee. Add relevant evidence and explain its function.
hints: Consider the committee's responsibility.
What would establish practical cost?
questions.answer: A priced estimate for preparing and updating ingredient labels would help the committee assess whether the safety proposal is financially feasible.

notes.title: Claims, reasons and audience in depth
paragraphs: A rhetorical situation joins a speaker, an audience, a purpose and circumstances that make the message necessary. The same fact can support different appeals because readers have different responsibilities. A claim states the judgement the audience is asked to accept; a reason explains why, and evidence makes the reason credible. An appeal to shared values is not automatically manipulation, but it cannot replace evidence about practical effects. Analyse the connection between a specific choice and a specific audience rather than labelling every emotional word as effective.

workedExamples.prompt: Original invented notice: 'Keep the drinking fountain open after practice; our evening teams should not have to buy water.' Explain the appeal to the school board.
steps: The proposal is continued access after practice, and the reason concerns equal access for evening teams.
The reference to buying water frames the decision as a cost imposed on some pupils; a board would also need maintenance and staffing information.
workedExamples.conclusion: The notice links fairness to a concrete policy while leaving implementation costs unproved.

flashcards.back: The situation that creates a need for a response.

flashcards.front: What separates a reason from evidence?
flashcards.back: A reason explains the claim; evidence supports that explanation.
Audience responsibilities help explain persuasive choices.

flashcards.front: Does an emotional appeal prove a claim?
flashcards.back: No; its factual reasoning still needs examination.

diagrams.title: Fountain access argument
diagrams.description: The argument connects a policy request to a fairness concern.

nodes.label: Evening closure
nodes.detail: Teams lose access after practice.

nodes.label: Unequal expense
nodes.detail: Some pupils must purchase water.

nodes.label: Extended access
nodes.detail: The proposed remedy addresses that expense.

modules.title: Thesis and reasoning structure
modules.focus: Make a defensible claim that directs the argument.
explanation: A thesis states a position that a reader could reasonably dispute. It should address the question and establish a direction for the reasoning. A list of topics or a promise to discuss an issue does not yet make an argument.

A line of reasoning connects claims in a deliberate sequence. Paragraphs should build rather than merely repeat. Choose evidence for its role: one example may establish a problem, while another tests the practicality of a proposed response.

workedExample.prompt: Revise “This essay discusses public gardens” into an arguable thesis.
steps: Choose a position: cities should prioritise gardens in underserved neighbourhoods.
Add reasoning: this allocation addresses unequal access more effectively than distributing sites evenly by area.

misconception.claim: A thesis must contain exactly three reasons.
misconception.correction: Its shape should serve the argument rather than a fixed numerical formula.

questions.prompt: Why is “Transport is important” a weak thesis?
questions.answer: It is broad and offers little direction; a specific policy claim with a reason would guide the argument.

questions.prompt: What should follow evidence that a bus route is overcrowded?
questions.answer: Commentary connecting crowding to the proposed change, with attention to whether added frequency would address the cause.

questions.prompt: Revise 'Homework is an issue' into a thesis about a specific policy and reason.
questions.hint: Select an action rather than a topic.
hints: Select an action rather than a topic.
State why that action matters.
questions.answer: Teachers should coordinate major homework deadlines because clustering them on one evening limits pupils' ability to plan sustained work.

questions.prompt: An essay supports deadline coordination but includes a paragraph describing classroom paint colours. Explain a useful revision.
questions.hint: Ask how the paragraph supports the central claim.
hints: Ask how the paragraph supports the central claim.
Replace irrelevant description with evidence about scheduling.
questions.answer: Replace the colour paragraph with evidence of clustered deadlines and explain how coordination could reduce that clustering; retain colour details only if a supported connection emerges.
checkpoints: Explain its role in the thesis.

notes.title: Thesis and reasoning structure in depth
paragraphs: An effective thesis is narrow enough to organise an essay and debatable enough to need support. Its reasons should answer why the claim follows, rather than merely announce the next topics. Each body paragraph then has a local claim connected to that main judgement. Evidence can support a reason, but a paragraph must explain the connection. A useful revision test is to ask whether changing a paragraph's conclusion would force a change in the thesis; if nothing changes, the paragraph may be background rather than necessary reasoning.

workedExamples.prompt: Revise the invented thesis 'School lunches have many aspects' into an argument with two connected reasons.
steps: Choose a specific decision: offer one low-cost vegetarian meal every day.
Supply relevant reasons: it increases dietary choice and allows pupils to compare options without a price penalty.
workedExamples.conclusion: Schools should offer a low-cost vegetarian meal daily because consistent availability and equal pricing make dietary choice more accessible.

flashcards.back: It offers a supportable judgement that reasonable readers could contest.
A paragraph's particular contribution to the main argument.

flashcards.front: Why is a list of topics insufficient?
flashcards.back: It does not explain their logical relationship.
The evidence, the paragraph's claim and the thesis.

diagrams.title: From evidence to thesis
diagrams.description: A lunch-pricing argument needs a connecting reason.

nodes.label: Price comparison
nodes.detail: The vegetarian meal costs more in the sample menu.

nodes.label: Barrier to choice
nodes.detail: The premium can constrain pupils with fixed budgets.

nodes.label: Equal-price proposal
nodes.detail: Removing the premium may widen practical choice.

modules.title: Sources and causal reasoning
modules.focus: Integrate evidence without overstating what it proves.
explanation: Synthesis brings sources into a conversation around your own claim. Attribute evidence clearly and explain agreement, tension or different scope. A paragraph that merely lists source summaries leaves the reader to infer the argument.

Causal reasoning needs more than sequence. If an outcome follows a policy, alternative causes may still matter. Use careful language that matches the evidence, distinguishing association from a demonstrated mechanism or controlled comparison.

workedExample.prompt: A town installs cycle lanes and shop revenue later rises. Evaluate the claim that lanes caused all the growth.
steps: The sequence makes the explanation possible but not established.
Check wider economic trends, other street improvements and comparisons before assigning causation.

misconception.claim: Two sources that disagree cannot both be useful.
misconception.correction: Their differences can reveal distinct assumptions, populations or competing explanations.

questions.prompt: How can a writer use two surveys with different age groups responsibly?
questions.answer: Describe each sample and avoid combining their results as if they measured the same population.

questions.prompt: Why is a quotation insufficient without commentary?
questions.hint: Consider the link to your thesis.
questions.answer: Readers need an explanation of how the quoted evidence supports, qualifies or challenges the argument.

questions.prompt: An invented survey of cycling-club members finds 90% favour new cycle racks. What population does it describe directly?
hints: Look at recruitment.
Distinguish club members from all residents.
questions.answer: It directly describes the surveyed club members, not all residents; cycling interest could make their preferences unrepresentative.

questions.prompt: Two fictional schools introduce tutoring; only one also extends library hours. Scores rise more at that school. What causal limitation follows?
questions.hint: List the changes that differ between schools.
hints: List the changes that differ between schools.
Can the observed gain isolate tutoring?
questions.answer: The difference cannot isolate tutoring because library hours also changed and may affect study; compare equivalent conditions or acknowledge the competing explanation.
checkpoints: State a suitable limitation or comparison.

notes.title: Sources and causal reasoning in depth
paragraphs: Causal reasoning requires more than events occurring together. Reverse causation, a common cause and selective sampling can all produce an association. Writers should distinguish the observation from the explanation proposed for it. Sources also differ in purpose and method: a firsthand account can reveal one person's experience without estimating prevalence, while a representative survey can describe a distribution without explaining every motive. Integrating sources means using each for the claim its design can support. Attribution and a clear account of limitations strengthen reasoning rather than automatically weakening it.

workedExamples.prompt: Invented data: pupils who attend optional writing workshops submit more essays. Assess a claim that workshops alone caused the increase.
steps: Attendance may reflect prior motivation, which could also increase submissions.
Compare prior submission patterns and relevant conditions; a randomised offer could help test an effect, but attendance data alone cannot.
workedExamples.conclusion: The association supports further investigation, not the claim that the workshop caused every additional essay.

flashcards.back: The proposed outcome may influence the proposed cause.
A factor related to both proposed cause and outcome.
A documented account, not a population rate.
Readers need its source, population and measurement context.

diagrams.title: Motivation as a common cause
diagrams.description: A third variable can explain an apparent workshop effect.

nodes.label: Prior motivation
nodes.detail: Some pupils already practise more.

nodes.label: Workshop attendance
nodes.detail: Motivated pupils may choose extra sessions.

nodes.label: Higher submissions
nodes.detail: Attendance is associated with an outcome also influenced by motivation.

modules.title: Introductions, definitions and conclusions
modules.focus: Frame the issue so the reader can assess the claim.
explanation: An introduction establishes the problem and stakes before presenting a claim. Definitions matter when a key term has competing meanings: a policy argument about access changes if access means physical entry, affordability or meaningful participation.

Comparison can clarify a proposal by holding one dimension constant. Conclusions should explain the significance of the reasoning or its implications, rather than introduce unsupported evidence or merely repeat every sentence of the introduction.

workedExample.prompt: A proposal claims a museum is accessible because admission is free. Test the definition.
steps: Free admission establishes financial access.
Transport, opening hours and physical design may still restrict other forms of access.

misconception.claim: Defining a term is neutral and never affects an argument.
misconception.correction: A definition can include some experiences and exclude others, shaping the conclusion.

questions.prompt: How could an introduction establish stakes for a water-conservation argument?
questions.answer: It could explain local supply pressure and the decisions households or authorities face before stating the proposal.

questions.prompt: What makes a comparison of two school policies fairer?
questions.answer: Use the same outcome and comparable conditions while acknowledging relevant differences in resources or populations.

questions.prompt: An essay calls a bus service reliable because its buses look new. Explain the definitional problem.
hints: Distinguish appearance from performance.
What would passengers mean by reliable?
questions.answer: New appearance does not measure reliable operation; on-time arrivals, cancellations and consistency would better address whether passengers can depend on the service.

questions.prompt: Write a conclusion for an invented trial that increased participation but has no cost data.
hints: Retain the supported finding.
State what a funding decision still needs.
questions.answer: The trial supports expanding access through additional sessions, but a permanent funding decision needs operating-cost evidence alongside the participation gains.
checkpoints: Connect the limitation to the decision.

notes.title: Introductions, definitions and conclusions in depth
paragraphs: An introduction gives readers enough context to recognise a decision, its stakes and the terms on which it will be judged. Definitions can be argumentative: defining success as attendance privileges a different outcome from defining it as learning. A fair definition is explicit, relevant and applied consistently. Conclusions should show what the reasoning permits readers to decide, rather than merely repeat the opening. They may identify a consequence or unresolved condition, but introducing an unsupported major claim at the end creates a new burden the essay has not met.

workedExamples.prompt: An invented debate calls a youth centre successful because visits increased. Refine the judgement.
steps: Separate attendance from the centre's stated aim of improving access to supervised activities.
Ask who attended, which activities were available and whether excluded groups gained access.
workedExamples.conclusion: Rising visits is useful evidence of use, but success requires measures aligned with the centre's purpose.

flashcards.back: Different meanings can conceal disagreement about the outcome.
The consequences that make a decision matter.

flashcards.front: What should a conclusion follow from?
flashcards.back: The argument and evidence already developed.

flashcards.front: Can a measure become a definition?
flashcards.back: Only if the writer justifies that it represents the intended concept.

diagrams.title: Defining centre success
diagrams.description: A broad aim becomes an assessable judgement through an explicit measure.

nodes.label: Access aim
nodes.detail: More young people can use supervised activities.

nodes.label: Relevant measures
nodes.detail: Track participation by group and available sessions.

nodes.label: Qualified judgement
nodes.detail: Attendance growth counts when it reflects wider access.

modules.title: Commentary, qualifiers and transitions
modules.focus: Show the logical relationship between sentences.
explanation: Commentary explains why evidence matters. Move beyond “this proves” by identifying a mechanism, assumption or implication. Qualifiers such as “under these conditions” can make a claim more accurate by specifying its range rather than weakening it automatically.

Transitions should name the relationship between ideas: contrast, consequence, extension or concession. A connective cannot repair a missing logical link. Check whether each paragraph advances the thesis and whether the evidence warrants the degree of certainty.

workedExample.prompt: Original evidence: “Weekend attendance doubled after free entry.” Write cautious commentary.
steps: Explain that removing admission costs may have reduced one barrier.
Qualify the inference because publicity or seasonal events may also have affected attendance.

misconception.correction: Precise limitations can make a claim more defensible.

questions.prompt: Why is “therefore” misleading between two unrelated facts?
questions.answer: It implies that one establishes the other, even when no supporting relationship has been shown.

questions.prompt: Revise “Online lessons work for everyone” responsibly.
questions.answer: Online lessons can support some learners when access, suitable teaching and independent-study support are available.

questions.prompt: Join these invented claims accurately: 'The shorter form reduced completion time. Some users found its instructions unclear.'
questions.hint: One result does not erase the other.
hints: One result does not erase the other.
Choose a contrast transition.
questions.answer: The shorter form reduced completion time; however, some users found its instructions unclear, so speed alone does not establish overall usability.

questions.prompt: Revise 'The survey proves nobody wants printed notices' when 8 of 12 respondents preferred email.
questions.hint: Check both the fraction and the sampled group.
hints: Check both the fraction and the sampled group.
Preference is not rejection of every alternative.
questions.answer: Eight of twelve respondents preferred email; this sample suggests demand for digital notices but does not show universal opposition to print.

notes.title: Commentary, qualifiers and transitions in depth
paragraphs: Commentary articulates the inference that turns information into evidence for a claim. A transition should name a real relationship: addition, contrast, concession or consequence. Substituting 'therefore' for explanation leaves the inference unproved. Qualifiers such as 'in this sample' and 'under these conditions' specify scope; vague hedging such as 'maybe somehow' does not. Effective qualification preserves the strongest claim the evidence warrants. Read a paragraph with its quotations removed: the remaining commentary should still reveal the writer's reasoning, even though the support would then be missing.

workedExamples.prompt: Invented evidence: 24 of 30 users found a sign easier to read after larger lettering. Write commentary with an appropriate qualifier.
steps: Compute that four fifths of this small user group preferred the larger lettering.
Connect readability to the change without assuming the same response for every reader or setting.
workedExamples.conclusion: In this trial, larger lettering improved reported readability for most participants, supporting further testing with a broader group.

flashcards.back: A contrast or qualification.
A defensible inferential connection.
The people, settings or conditions a claim covers.

flashcards.front: How does commentary differ from paraphrase?
flashcards.back: It explains why evidence matters to the argument.

diagrams.title: A bounded readability inference
diagrams.description: The conclusion retains both the finding and its limits.

nodes.label: 24 of 30 respondents
nodes.detail: Most trial participants preferred larger text.

nodes.label: Reported readability
nodes.detail: Preference is evidence about their reading experience.

nodes.label: Broader testing
nodes.detail: Other users and settings remain untested.

modules.title: Perspective, bias and revision
modules.focus: Let new evidence change the shape of an argument.
explanation: A position is the claim someone supports; perspective includes the experiences and assumptions from which they view the issue. People may share a position for different reasons. Bias should be examined through evidence selection and reasoning, not used as a label that ends discussion.

A writer can revise a claim when new evidence identifies a limitation. Tone also affects reception: a shift from accusation to concession may invite a sceptical audience to consider a proposal without requiring agreement on every premise.

workedExample.prompt: A writer supports a car-free street, then learns that some residents need vehicle access.
steps: Acknowledge the access need as relevant evidence.
Revise the proposal to consider exemptions or alternatives, and assess whether they preserve its intended benefit.

misconception.claim: Recognising an opposing concern means abandoning the argument.
misconception.correction: A justified adjustment can preserve the central claim while addressing real limits.

questions.prompt: Why examine a campaign group’s funding when reading its report?
questions.answer: Funding may illuminate interests that shape framing; the report’s methods and evidence still need direct evaluation.

questions.prompt: How can tone change without changing the basic policy position?
questions.answer: The writer can replace dismissive language with respectful acknowledgement while continuing to support the same proposal.

questions.prompt: A fictional recycling company funds a waste report. Explain how to evaluate it without dismissing it solely for funding.
hints: Funding can reveal an interest.
Inspect sampling and measurement.
questions.answer: Identify the company's interest, examine how waste was sampled and counted, and compare relevant independent measurements before deciding how much weight to give the report.

questions.prompt: A writer proposes digital-only homework, then learns some pupils share one device. Make a substantive revision.
hints: Identify the access consequence.
Modify the policy, not just the tone.
questions.answer: Offer equivalent offline work or reliable device access before requiring digital submission, because shared devices can prevent pupils from meeting the same deadlines.

notes.title: Perspective, bias and revision in depth
paragraphs: Perspective concerns the position from which a source sees a problem; bias concerns systematic influences on selection or interpretation. Neither a stated affiliation nor a personal experience automatically makes evidence worthless. Evaluate the methods and what the source leaves out. Revision becomes substantive when new evidence changes the claim, its conditions or the proposed action. Changing only the vocabulary while keeping an unsupported generalisation is cosmetic. A responsible argument can retain a policy preference while acknowledging an affected group's needs and modifying the implementation to address them.

workedExamples.prompt: A fictional sports organiser praises a new booking app, but a participant reports that its screen reader labels are missing. Revise the assessment.
steps: The organiser's faster scheduling supports administrative convenience, while the participant identifies an access barrier.
Add accessible labelling and test with users before presenting the app as suitable for everyone.
workedExamples.conclusion: The app can simplify booking, conditional on resolving and checking the accessibility problem.

flashcards.back: No; inspect its method and relevance.
It changes reasoning, scope or action in response to evidence.

flashcards.front: What can a marginalised perspective reveal?
flashcards.back: A consequence omitted from the dominant account.
A well-meant policy may still impose an unexamined burden.

diagrams.title: Revising an app recommendation
diagrams.description: A second perspective changes implementation conditions.

nodes.label: Administrative gain
nodes.detail: Booking takes less staff time.

nodes.label: Access barrier
nodes.detail: Unlabelled controls obstruct a screen reader.

nodes.label: Conditional recommendation
nodes.detail: Repair and test access before wider adoption.

modules.title: Counterarguments and qualified claims
modules.focus: Test the argument against its strongest reasonable challenge.
explanation: A useful counterargument represents a plausible objection accurately. Concession accepts a valid part; rebuttal explains why the main claim still holds under relevant conditions. Refuting an exaggerated version of an opponent’s view creates a straw person rather than a serious test.

Sentence structure can express complexity. A subordinate clause may acknowledge a limit while a main clause states the principal judgement. Ensure the grammar reflects the actual priority of ideas instead of hiding a major unresolved problem.

workedExample.prompt: Original claim: “Extend park hours.” Objection: “Lighting and staffing cost money.”
steps: Concede that operating costs are real.
Argue for a limited trial only if projected access benefits justify the measured costs.

misconception.claim: Mentioning any opposing opinion counts as addressing a counterargument.
misconception.correction: The response must explain how the objection affects the reasoning.

questions.prompt: Why is “Opponents hate public space” a weak response?
questions.answer: It attacks an invented motive rather than addressing their actual concern, such as safety or expense.

questions.prompt: Complete a qualified claim about later school starts.
questions.answer: Later starts may support sleep opportunities, but transport and family schedules must be considered in implementation.

questions.prompt: Original invented objection: 'Longer lessons could tire younger pupils.' Write a fair concession without abandoning longer lessons entirely.
hints: Accept a plausible limit.
Specify a condition worth testing.
questions.answer: Longer sessions may tire younger pupils, so a trial should include breaks and measure engagement before any general extension.

questions.prompt: Why does 'Anyone opposing a quiet study room hates learning' fail as rebuttal? Supply a stronger response to a cost objection.
hints: Separate motive from argument.
Compare the proposed benefit with the cost.
questions.answer: The sentence invents opponents' motives; a stronger response would compare the room's use and staffing expense with alternative ways to provide quiet space.

notes.title: Counterarguments and qualified claims in depth
paragraphs: A counterargument is a reasoned challenge to a claim, its evidence or its consequences. Represent its strongest relevant form before responding. A concession accepts a valid part of the challenge; a rebuttal explains why it does not overturn the final judgement. Sometimes the strongest response is a narrower proposal. Avoid presenting objections as moral defects in opponents. The argument gains credibility when readers can see what evidence would change the recommendation and why the revised conditions address the challenge rather than merely restating the original position.

workedExamples.prompt: Invented proposal: require reusable lunch boxes. Objection: some families cannot afford an initial purchase. Develop a qualified response.
steps: Accept that upfront cost can make an otherwise useful policy unequal.
Add a free lending scheme and evaluate cleaning capacity before requiring participation.
workedExamples.conclusion: A reusable-box policy is defensible only if access and cleaning arrangements prevent the cost saving from excluding families.

flashcards.back: Acceptance of a valid part of an opposing argument.
A distorted, weaker version of the actual objection.
Yes, by making its conditions defensible.
The objection's reason or evidence.

diagrams.title: Cost objection and policy revision
diagrams.description: The objection produces a concrete condition.

nodes.label: Reuse proposal
nodes.detail: Reduce disposable lunch packaging.

nodes.label: Upfront cost
nodes.detail: Purchase requirements may exclude families.

nodes.label: Loan provision
nodes.detail: Remove the barrier before requiring reuse.

modules.title: Style and audience relationships
modules.focus: Explain how word and sentence choices shape credibility.
explanation: Style includes diction, syntax, imagery and rhythm. Analyse a choice in context: short sentences can convey urgency, but they can also suggest simplicity, certainty or restraint. Its function depends on the surrounding argument and audience.

An analogy can make an unfamiliar idea accessible, but it also selects which similarities matter. Evaluate both its explanatory value and its limits. Avoid treating a vivid comparison as independent proof of a policy claim.

workedExample.prompt: Original line: “A public timetable is a promise, not a decoration.” Explain its effect.
steps: The contrast recasts scheduling as an obligation to passengers.
Its concise structure emphasises accountability, though service evidence is still needed to support a criticism.

misconception.claim: Naming a rhetorical device is sufficient analysis.
misconception.correction: Explain what the specific choice does for this argument and audience.

questions.prompt: Why might technical jargon reduce credibility with a general audience?
questions.answer: Unexplained terms can obscure the reasoning and make readers feel excluded, even when the information is accurate.

questions.prompt: How should a writer test an analogy between a city budget and a household budget?
questions.answer: Identify limits such as borrowing powers and public responsibilities before treating household constraints as equivalent.

questions.prompt: Original invented line: 'Read the map, check the route, ask the driver.' Identify the structure and a plausible effect in travel advice.
hints: Compare the verb forms.
Consider the practical sequence.
questions.answer: Three parallel imperatives make the actions easy to follow and give the advice a direct, practical tone.

questions.prompt: Rewrite 'Our infrastructure exhibits substantial modal integration deficiencies' for residents, preserving meaning. Explain the choice.
questions.hint: Replace abstract jargon with concrete travel language.
hints: Replace abstract jargon with concrete travel language.
Retain the connection between transport modes.
questions.answer: 'Our buses and trains do not connect well.' Naming familiar services makes the problem clearer to residents while retaining the criticism of poor connections.

notes.title: Style and audience relationships in depth
paragraphs: Style shapes the relationship a writer offers an audience. Parallel syntax can make alternatives comparable; a short sentence after a long one can concentrate emphasis. Diction may invite shared responsibility or distance the writer from readers. Effects depend on context: technical precision helps specialists but may require explanation for others. Naming a device is only the start of analysis. Identify the relevant wording, explain what it emphasises, and connect that effect to the argument's purpose. Avoid claiming that every reader will necessarily experience the same emotion.

workedExamples.prompt: Original invented speech: 'We measured the queues. We counted the missed buses. We still ignored the people waiting.' Analyse its structure.
steps: The repeated 'We' and parallel clauses connect the speaker to the institution's actions.
The final clause shifts from measurement to failure, suggesting that collecting data did not guarantee care.
workedExamples.conclusion: Parallelism makes the gap between administrative knowledge and responsibility the speech's emphasis.

flashcards.back: Repeated grammatical structure across related elements.
They position speaker, audience and other groups.

flashcards.front: Does a device have one fixed effect?
flashcards.back: No; wording and rhetorical context determine its function.
A textual choice linked to a plausible audience effect and purpose.

diagrams.title: From repetition to accountability
diagrams.description: A repeated subject builds a cumulative criticism.

nodes.label: 'We measured'
nodes.detail: The institution possessed information.

nodes.label: 'We counted'
nodes.detail: Further evidence reinforces that knowledge.

nodes.label: 'We still ignored'
nodes.detail: The contrast shifts attention to responsibility.

modules.title: Synthesis and a nuanced final argument
modules.focus: Reconcile evidence while keeping a clear judgement.
explanation: A complex argument recognises genuine tensions without becoming indecisive. Establish the conditions under which a claim holds and explain why one consideration deserves more weight. The conclusion should follow from the evidence rather than from an assumed compromise.

When synthesising, organise by reasons or questions rather than one paragraph per source. Concede valid evidence, rebut unsupported inferences and preserve uncertainty where sources cannot settle an issue. Distinguish your reasoning from the statements you attribute.

workedExample.prompt: One source shows pedestrian safety gains; another reports delivery difficulties after a street closure.
steps: Treat both as evidence about different outcomes.
Develop a conditional proposal, such as restricted delivery windows, and explain what further evaluation it needs.

misconception.claim: A nuanced argument must give every position equal weight.
misconception.correction: Weight should reflect evidence quality, relevance and the stakes of the decision.

questions.prompt: What distinguishes synthesis from a sequence of summaries?
questions.hint: Look for relationships and your claim.
questions.answer: Synthesis uses sources together to support or qualify a line of reasoning, explaining their agreements and tensions.

questions.prompt: How should a conclusion handle unresolved cost evidence?
questions.answer: State the limitation and identify the evidence needed before a firm cost judgement, while retaining supported conclusions.

questions.prompt: Two invented reports say a park gained visitors and nearby residents experienced more noise. Explain why the findings need not contradict each other.
questions.hint: Identify the outcome in each source.
hints: Identify the outcome in each source.
Can both change at the same time?
questions.answer: Visitor numbers and neighbourhood noise measure different outcomes; both can rise, so a recommendation must weigh access benefits alongside residents' disturbance.

questions.prompt: Develop a qualified recommendation from that park evidence without inventing new findings.
hints: Address both outcomes.
Treat the remedy as a proposal requiring evaluation.
questions.answer: Keep the park accessible while trialling quieter evening activities and monitoring noise; the current evidence supports addressing disturbance but does not establish which remedy will work.

notes.title: Synthesis and a nuanced final argument in depth
paragraphs: Synthesis organises sources around a question rather than giving each source an isolated paragraph. Sources may agree on one outcome while disagreeing about another, or use different populations and timeframes. Keep those distinctions visible. A nuanced argument makes a judgement after weighing the tension; it does not end with an empty statement that both sides have points. Specify which criteria matter, how the evidence bears on them and what remains uncertain. A final proposal may combine elements from competing positions when the combination addresses a documented trade-off.

workedExamples.prompt: Invented sources: a survey reports demand for evening classes; a staffing memo says the building cannot open every night. Synthesize a recommendation.
steps: The survey establishes an access demand, while the memo limits feasible frequency.
Propose two evenings on a trial basis and measure attendance against staffing costs.
workedExamples.conclusion: A limited evening programme addresses the demand while testing the operational constraint that prevents an immediate daily expansion.

flashcards.back: The writer's question and line of reasoning.
Different samples may explain apparently conflicting findings.
An action justified only under stated conditions.
No; it requires a judgement that accounts for important complications.

diagrams.title: Demand meets capacity
diagrams.description: Two kinds of evidence shape one practical conclusion.

nodes.label: Evening demand
nodes.detail: Potential learners need later sessions.

nodes.label: Staffing limit
nodes.detail: Only two evenings are feasible initially.

nodes.label: Measured trial
nodes.detail: Test whether attendance justifies ongoing provision.
